short_answer: Stu Feiner is a real and well known figure. He has sold picks under his own name for decades, his site promotes his role on Barstool Sports Advisors, and his site lists prices and a phone number. In that narrow sense he is legitimate: you pay, and he sends picks.

Whether his paid picks make money is a different question, and nothing we could open answers it. His homepage shows win and loss totals for bet tiers such as "$100k Bet Record 146-126-2", with no dates, odds or pick log. The one outside test we found is old: Sports Illustrated monitored him for four weeks in 1991 and he went 19-32. The same article reported a 1990 New York City fine for false and misleading advertising.

Prices run far above most pick sellers, up to $50,000 for a season or a month, and we found no guarantee or refund terms. If you buy, start with the cheapest product, record every pick yourself with the line and time you received it, and judge it only after a few hundred picks.

guarantee: We found no guarantee on any stufeiner.com page we opened: no refund, no free extension and no credit if a package loses. The purchase steps are simple. Pay through PayPal, then call or contact Stu to receive the picks.

The only purchase terms we found are in the site footer, which says buyers agree not to pass the picks on to anyone and warns that sharing or reselling them will bring legal action. Note also how the tiers are built. The $99 "all picks for the current day" passes leave out the bigger best bets, while "Daily Picks" with every selection for the day costs $5,000. A buyer should know exactly which plays a package includes before paying.

claims_note: Take the homepage tier records at face value and do the math. They work out to about 53.7% winners for the $100k tier, 59.4% for the double net worth tier, 56.2% for the $50k tier and 51.7% for the $25K tier. The site shows no odds, so none of these can be turned into profit, and the $25K tier sits below the roughly 52.4% needed to break even at -110. No dates are given, so a buyer cannot tell what period the totals cover or whether every play is counted.

The start date also moves around. The About page says "Since 1982" and "over 30 years", the same page mentions a "37 year career", and the site banner says "since 1989". Some pages look out of date: the NFL Season Pass page still describes "the 2021-2022 season".
record: What a buyer can verify independently: very little, and none of it is recent. The only outside test of his picks we could open is from Sports Illustrated's 18 Nov 1991 issue. SI wrote that Feiner agreed to be monitored for four weeks that September, that he "unfailingly" gave SI his picks, and that he went 19-32, a 37% win rate, for an imaginary loss of $6,210 at $100 a unit. That is a short sample from 35 years ago and says nothing certain about his picks today.

Regulatory history, as reported by a major outlet: the same SI article said Feiner was fined $13,000 in February 1990 by the New York City Department of Consumer Affairs for false and misleading advertising. SI also reported that a later brochure advertised a "1991 documented record college and pro: 9-3" while he was 19-32 in SI's test, and quoted Feiner saying that was his record before SI started documenting him. We did not find the department's own record of the fine, and we found no court or regulator action involving him in our searches today.

What Feiner himself publishes: tier totals on the homepage and short runs on the daily pick schedule. We found no full, time stamped log of every paid pick with the line, the odds and the release time on any page we could open without paying. His free picks on Barstool Sports Advisors are public, but we did not find a complete graded record of them either.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition no Stu Feiner pick account is matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how his picks perform.
our_data.context: For scale: Stu's own homepage tier records range from about 52% to 59% winners, with no odds shown. On the Watchdog board on 7 Nov 2026, {{over60}} of {{established}} established accounts (100 or more graded picks) were at 60% or better, and the median established account won {{median_win}}% of its picks. At standard -110 odds a bettor needs about 52.4% to break even.

customers_intro: Independent customer evidence on Stu Feiner's paid picks is thin. He is far better known as a media personality than as a reviewed service, and most of what we found is opinion, not buyer experience. A few people say they bought his picks; their reports are below, along with forum opinion and how much weight each can carry.

customers.text: On TheRX forum, a member said Feiner had gone 10-1 over two weeks of NFL picks shown on Barstool Sports Advisors and was "way above .500" the season before. He posted some of the winning picks but no full log, and we did not verify the figures.

In the same thread, another member said he had followed Feiner's picks over his whole career and wanted no part of him, and claimed that Feiner's old sales pitch told buyers to bet everything they owned. A third member replied that any capper can get hot for two weeks. None of this came with records, and we did not verify it.

A CapperTek reviewer said he paid for Feiner's college and pro football picks one weekend, went 0-5 on Saturday and 1-4 on Sunday, found no mention of the losses on the site or videos, and got no reply to emails. He said he would ask his bank to reverse the charge.
Another CapperTek reviewer said he had tried the picks and followed them for years, and claimed they lose over time while one good weekend gets promoted for weeks. He gave no record.

On TheRX, a member said calling the free pick line got him an offer of a $1,500 package for $299, that he bought it, and that Feiner had been "killing it". He posted no record, and the thread starter replied that the free line pushed him to a sales office instead of giving a free pick.
A TheRX member said Feiner pressed him on the phone to put $5,000 on a baseball season package and called him cheap when he declined, then gave him a guaranteed free playoff pick that lost.

On the Sportsbook Review forum, a member said he bought Feiner's service in his early betting days, received a multi team round robin, and had to mail back a signed credit card slip to the Farmingdale office. He said he wished he had bet against the picks. Other members in the thread called Feiner a scammer without giving evidence.

In a TheRX thread, members called Feiner and another tout scam artists and said their offices kept calling people who had given a phone number. None of this came with records, and we did not verify it.
In another TheRX thread, members said his records were not true and claimed that pricey private plays went bad once they were released. No one posted a log, and we did not verify it.
A Trustpilot company search for Stu Feiner showed no listing for him or his site.
A Better Business Bureau search for Stu Feiner returned no results.
The betting subreddit posts we read since 2024 never mention him. We found no testimonials on stufeiner.com and no app store listing for his picks.

conflicts: We saw no sportsbook affiliate links, promo codes or revenue share offers on the stufeiner.com pages we opened. The site sells picks, Cameo and custom shoutout videos, and merchandise through a separate store.

His site promotes Barstool Sports Advisors and sells a package named after the show. A buyer should know that his public picks are part of an entertainment show as well as a sales funnel for his paid packages.
strengths: A real, public person with a long on camera history, a working phone line on the contact page and a published price list.
His free picks on Barstool Sports Advisors let a bettor watch his style before paying, and the cheapest packages cost $55 to $99.
In the one outside test we found, SI credited him for giving them every pick during monitoring.
concerns: No full public record. The homepage tier totals have no dates or odds, and by his own numbers the $25K tier wins about 51.7%, below break even at -110.
No guarantee or refund terms found, on packages that run up to $50,000.
The cheap daily passes leave out the bigger best bets, which are sold separately for $1,000 to $5,000 each.
Sports Illustrated reported a 1990 New York City fine for false and misleading advertising and a 19-32 result in its 1991 test. Both are old, but they are the only outside evidence we found.
Career start dates differ from page to page, and some product pages are out of date.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Most "guarantees" in this business are credits.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: He is a real, well known handicapper who sells picks under his own name with published prices and a phone number. We could not verify that his paid picks win over time, and Sports Illustrated reported in 1991 that New York City fined him in 1990 for false and misleading advertising.
How much does Stu Feiner cost?

On 7 Nov 2026 his packages ran from $55 (five picks) and $99 daily passes up to $1,000 to $5,000 for single best bets, $15,000 for a week, and $50,000 for the November package or a season pass. We found no guarantee or refund terms.
Does Stu Feiner have a verified record?

No current one that we could find. His homepage shows win and loss totals by bet tier with no dates, odds or log, and the only outside test we opened is a four week Sports Illustrated check in 1991, where he went 19-32.

For the money you get his picks and his best bet ratings from a famous name, with a cheap $55 to $99 entry point. What is unproven is whether those picks beat the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over hundreds of plays, and nothing protects you if a package loses.
